Alphabet's Q3 capex hit $51 billion, up 114% year over year, pushing free cash flow to negative $9 billion for the second straight quarter.

Alphabet's $0.22 quarterly dividend consumes just 7% of operating cash flow and was protected while buybacks were suspended entirely.

Meta also reported negative free cash flow with no buybacks, while Microsoft kept free cash flow positive and returned $10 billion to shareholders.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Google made the cut. Enter your email to see the other nine names and why GOOGL earned its spot. The report is free. Enter your email and see the full list.

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) shares fell roughly 12% in today's session to around $285. The third-quarter report showed free cash flow turning negative for the second quarter in a row. Business Insider described the selloff as a wipeout of market value following the earnings miss. Income investors now have a narrower question: can a company spending more than it brings in keep paying its $0.22 quarterly dividend?

achinthamb
GOOGL Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Capex Now Outruns Operating Cash

In the third quarter, Alphabet spent $51.36 billion on capital expenditures, up 114.4% year over year. Operating cash flow was $42.29 billion, so free cash flow came in at negative $9.07 billion. That follows negative $5.86 billion in the second quarter. Management argues the demand justifies the spending:

"Google Cloud revenues grew 103%, powered by huge demand for our AI infrastructure and AI solutions. We're also seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers."

CEO Sundar Pichai said that on the October 28 call. Cloud operating income reached $11.12 billion, compared with $3.59 billion a year earlier.

AMD Has Ripped 170% This Year: Is It Too Late to Buy? ©@Alexander's Images via Canva, @Nicolas Foster from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD stock is up 170% in 2026, carried by two record data center quarters and Meta's deal for up to 6 gigawatts of its AI chips.

Intel ran nearly as far on demand for server chips, while Nvidia lagged and trades at less than half AMD's forward multiple.

October's AI-financing scare cut AMD's multiple while analysts kept expecting its normalized EPS to more than double in 2027.

The Nov. 3 report is the first test of that doubling, and if it holds, AMD isn't too late to buy.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) stock is up 170% in 2026, and the business earned most of it: two record data center quarters and a deal with Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) for up to 6 gigawatts of its Instinct GPUs.

The chip rally helped too. Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) is up 159% this year on the same hunger for server chips, while Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) has gained just 15% and trades at well under half AMD's forward multiple. So what does AMD's premium pay for?

From a February stumble to two record quarters

The year started badly. On Feb. 3, AMD guided first-quarter revenue below the quarter it had just reported, and the stock lost 17% the next day.

Three weeks later, Meta signed on for up to 6 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs with a warrant for up to 160 million AMD shares.

Then the numbers showed up. First-quarter revenue came in at $10.25 billion, against the $9.89 billion analysts expected, with data center sales up 57%. In the second quarter, revenue rose 50% to $11.5 billion, data center sales more than doubled to $6.7 billion, and AMD guided to about $13 billion for the third quarter.

Intel's run rests on part of the same story. AMD raised its forecast for the 2030 server CPU market to about $220 billion, from about $60 billion, in nine months, as AI agents eat up CPUs. New Street Research upgraded Intel to Buy on Oct. 26, arguing that server CPU supply will stay tight for years, so Intel's third-quarter report, due before AMD's, is a read on AMD's server business.

October took some of the froth off

AMD closed at a record on Oct. 6, the day CEO Lisa Su said it would raise supply substantially in 2027. Then fears over who pays for AI data centers hit chip stocks, and AMD now sits [12%] below that high.

Alphabet trades near a P/E of 14 versus Meta's 22, backed by paying Cloud customers rather than a future bet on Muse becoming a commerce platform.

Meta's Muse agent drew over 10 million U.S. and Canadian users in six weeks, with more than 25% of weekly users already shopping through it.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Google made the cut. Enter your email to see the other nine names and why GOOGL earned its spot. The report is free. Enter your email and see the full list.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) both missed EPS estimates this month. In both cases, the miss came from items outside their ad businesses. Meta took a $9.89B legal charge. Alphabet recorded an $8.70B equity securities loss. Underneath those charges, both ad businesses grew quickly while AI capex jumped and free cash flow turned negative.

Kelly Sullivan / Getty Images Entertainment via Getty Images
Ad Pricing Carries Meta While Cloud Carries Alphabet

Meta's revenue rose 26.1% to $64.60B. Average price per ad climbed 14%, as advertisers paid more per ad. Nearly 10 million advertisers used a generative AI creative tool. Without the legal charge, operating income would have risen 11%. That is a healthy core hidden by a messy headline.

Alphabet's highlight was Google Cloud, where revenue rose 103% to $30.71B. Search still matters too. Sundar Pichai said "our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years." That answers the worry that AI chatbots would hollow out Search, at least for now.
